summary: Faropenem is an orally active penem (beta-lactam) antibacterial available in several countries (notably India and Japan) as faropenem sodium and the prodrug faropenem medoxomil. Like other beta-lactams it inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and has activity against many Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms, with stability against many beta-lactamases. It is used for respiratory, urinary, skin and soft-tissue, and other community infections. Typical adult oral doses are 150-300 mg two to three times daily. Faropenem is not FDA-approved.

moa: Faropenem is a penem beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis by binding to and inactivating penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), leading to defective cell-wall formation and bacterial lysis. Its penem structure confers stability against many beta-lactamases (including some extended-spectrum and AmpC enzymes) and resistance to renal dehydropeptidase-I, so it does not require a dehydropeptidase inhibitor like cilastatin. It exhibits time-dependent (time-above-MIC) bactericidal activity against susceptible Gram-positive cocci, many Gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobes.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to faropenem or other penem/carbapenem antibiotics
History of severe hypersensitivity (e.g. anaphylaxis) to beta-lactam antibiotics
relative: History of penicillin or cephalosporin allergy (risk of cross-reactivity)
Patients with predisposition to seizures (class effect of beta-lactams)
monitor: Signs of hypersensitivity reaction, especially with first doses
Diarrhoea suggestive of Clostridioides difficile infection
Renal function in those with impairment
Clinical response and resolution of infection

preg: There are limited human data on faropenem in pregnancy. Use only if the expected benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, in line with the local product information. Beta-lactams as a class are generally considered relatively safe, but specific data for faropenem are insufficient.
lact: Data on excretion of faropenem in human breast milk are limited. Use with caution during breastfeeding, weighing the benefit of treatment against potential effects on the infant (e.g. altered gut flora, diarrhoea, candidiasis).
renal: Faropenem is eliminated largely by the kidneys, so reduce the dose or extend the dosing interval in moderate to severe renal impairment according to product labeling. Monitor renal function and clinical response; accumulation may increase the risk of adverse effects.
hepatic: Limited data are available in hepatic impairment. Use with caution and monitor liver enzymes, particularly on prolonged courses; transient elevations of transaminases have been reported.

major: Valproic acid / sodium valproate - penems and carbapenems can markedly reduce valproate plasma levels and precipitate seizures; avoid concomitant use
moderate: Probenecid - may reduce renal excretion and increase faropenem plasma levels
Other nephrotoxic agents - monitor renal function when co-administered
Live bacterial vaccines (e.g. oral typhoid) - antibacterials may reduce efficacy
minor: Bacteriostatic antibiotics - theoretical antagonism of bactericidal activity
Antacids - may modestly affect absorption; separate administration if needed
interactions.food: May be taken with food; food can improve tolerability and, for the medoxomil prodrug, absorption.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction reported; moderation is advised during any acute infection.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause a false-positive urine glucose test with non-enzymatic (copper-reduction) methods, as seen with other beta-lactams; transient rises in transaminases or eosinophils may occur.

serious: Seizures (class effect, especially with valproate or renal impairment)
emergency: Anaphylaxis or angioedema with airway compromise
Fulminant or severe C. difficile colitis

counsel: Take the medicine with or after food and complete the full course even if you feel better
Stop the medicine and seek urgent help if you develop a rash, facial or throat swelling, or difficulty breathing
Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhoea, which can occur during or after treatment
Tell your doctor if you have ever had an allergic reaction to penicillins, cephalosporins, or other beta-lactam antibiotics
Tell your doctor if you take valproate (an epilepsy medicine), as the combination should be avoided
Take doses at evenly spaced intervals to keep the medicine working effectively
pk: Bactericidal activity begins after absorption; clinical response over the course
Plasma peak approximately 0.5-1.5 h after an oral dose
Approximately 1 h (short; supports two- to three-times-daily dosing)
Time-above-MIC dependent; requires multiple daily doses
Store below 25-30 C, protected from moisture and light
pearls: Only orally active penem in clinical use; stable to renal dehydropeptidase so no cilastatin needed
Stability against many beta-lactamases (including some ESBL/AmpC) but it is NOT a substitute for carbapenems in serious resistant infections
Widely used in India/Japan; overuse has raised antimicrobial-stewardship concerns about driving carbapenem resistance
Avoid with valproate - penems/carbapenems can crash valproate levels and trigger seizures
Cross-reactivity possible in penicillin/cephalosporin-allergic patients; take an allergy history first
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule - do not take a double dose. Try to keep doses evenly spaced through the day.
overdose: Experience with faropenem overdose is limited. Expected effects are extensions of adverse reactions, mainly gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) and, with very high beta-lactam exposure or in renal impairment, potential central nervous system excitation including seizures. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with symptomatic care, control of seizures with benzodiazepines if they occur, and maintenance of hydration and renal function. Faropenem may be removed to some extent by haemodialysis in severe renal impairment.
